sweep_summary: Three target items. (1) Good 2004 Lingua (the catalog's deciding source) re-downloaded from the author's page — byte-identical to the catalog copy — and re-read: split lexicon, tonal classes with no stress, pitch accent class with stress derived from the leftmost H by trochaic parsing; catalog quote verbatim; confirms. (2) Good 'A twice-mixed creole?' (Glottolog 2006 ms = Studies in Language 33, 2009; listed by Glottolog as a dictionary is a Glottolog mis-typing) already held by the project as the author preprint; historical paper restating the same analysis (stress in pitch-accented words predictable from accent position; tonal words unmarked for accent); confirms. (3) Rountree 1994 Missiology is an ethnographic piece on proverbs/wisdom literature — not relevant, paywalled SAGE DOI, priority none. Beyond the list: the primary source of the catalog's stress rule, Rountree 1972b 'The phonological structure of stems in Saramaccan' (Grimes ed., Languages of the Guianas, SIL 1972, pp. 22-27), was located as an open Rosetta Project scan on archive.org and read first-hand; its pp. 25-26 stress rule (first long syllable of the foot, else penult of the foot; leftmost stress heaviest; disyllabic LH stems vary) matches Good's block quote exactly, so the catalog locator can cite Rountree 1972b: 25-26 directly instead of 'as quoted by Good'. Good 2005 (J. Portuguese Linguistics, held by the project) gives the crispest formulation of the stress-from-accent algorithm (p. 11). catalog's classification 'tonal' / tonal-OR-pitch accent stands; nothing read contradicts it. Only unread candidate: McWhorter & Good 2012 grammar ch. 2 'Prosodic phonology' (De Gruyter, paywalled, priority low — same co-author, expected to restate Good 2004). all look-ups went through Crossref/Glottolog/archive.org downloads. new_statements.quote: The stress pattern of stems can be predicted according to the following rules. (1) The first long syllable in each foot of the stem is stressed. (2) If there is no long syllable, the next to the last syllable in the phonological foot is stressed. In simple stems that correspond to more than one phonological foot, the first stress is the heaviest. Compound stems remain to be investigated. Two-syllable stems with a LH tone pattern have no set pattern; the stress varies freely between the syllables: 'bebe ~ be'be 'drink', 'guli ~ gu'li 'swallow', 'kini ~ ki'ni 'knee'.
new_statements.citation: Rountree, S. Catherine. 1972. The phonological structure of stems in Saramaccan. In Joseph E. Grimes (ed.), Languages of the Guianas (SIL Publications in Linguistics 35), 22-27. Norman: SIL / University of Oklahoma.
new_statements.reading: First-hand SIL field description (1968-69, Upper Suriname River dialect). Tone: 'Every vowel carries one tone. Two tones, high and low, are contrastive' (p. 25). Stress: predictable within the phonological foot — the first long (VV/diphthong) syllable of the foot, otherwise the penult of the foot; in multi-foot stems the first (leftmost) stress is strongest; disyllabic LH stems have free variation. This is the very passage the catalog currently holds only second-hand, as Good 2004's block quote (preprint p. 14); the first-hand text matches it. It supports the catalog's 'tonal' coding (tone is the lexical contrast; stress is a non-contrastive, derived property) and does not overturn Good 2004's reanalysis, in which stress exists only in the pitch accent class and follows from the leftmost H/accent (Good 2004 preprint p. 18: 'word stress can be predicted from the location of the leftmost high-tone TBU').

new_statements.quote: C'est la seule langue creole connue jusqu'a l'heure actuelle dans laquelle le ton est nettement distinctif. [...] le systeme complique qui comprend deux niveaux de ton, trois contours de ton et la duree des voyelles peut s'analyser comme un systeme de deux niveaux de tons (aigu et grave) relativement tres simple, dans lequel chaque syllabe ou mot doit porter un niveau du ton. [fn. 2:] Nous ne parlerons pas ici en detail de la difference entre une langue tonale (Saramaccan) et une langue a accent (Sranan). [...] En Saramaccan, la syllabe est porteuse de la hauteur tonale [...], tandis qu'en Sranan c'est le mot qui est porteur d'une difference de hauteur tonale.
new_statements.translation: It is the only creole language known to date in which tone is clearly distinctive. [...] the complicated system comprising two tone levels, three tone contours and vowel length can be analysed as a relatively very simple system of two tone levels (high and low), in which every syllable or word must carry a tone level. [fn. 2:] We will not discuss here in detail the difference between a tone language (Saramaccan) and an accent language (Sranan). [...] In Saramaccan it is the syllable that carries the pitch level [...], whereas in Sranan it is the word that carries a difference of pitch.
new_statements.citation: Voorhoeve, Jan. 1961. Le ton et la grammaire dans le Saramaccan. Word 17:146-163.
new_statements.locator: p. 146 (sec. 1 'Le but de cette etude' and footnote 2); PDF page 2
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the the Internet Archive T&F PDF; the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'Le ton et la grammaire dans le Saramaccan', cover page cites word 17:2, 146-163, DOI..11659750). The quoted sentences are at the text layerand 60-64 (p. 146, sec. 1) and fn. 2 at lines 67-78, verbatim apart from stripped diacritics and scanned 'Ia' for 'la' (reader normalised to 'la'). Read secs. 1-3 and the conclusion: the paper treats Saramaccan as a two-level tone language (aigu/grave), syllabe = tone-bearing unit, tone sandhi and syntaxeme-final lowering, tonal word-structure constraints; no word-stress placement rule anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent|stress|intensit: only fn. 2'…
new_statements.relation_note: Supports the catalog's tonal coding of Saramaccan (two contrastive level tones, syllable as tone-bearing unit) and explicitly classes Saramaccan as a tone language as opposed to an accent language (Sranan). It is silent on the derived, foot-based stress placement that Rountree 1972 (existing statement) describes and on Good 2004's pitch accent/tone lexical split; nothing in it contradicts either.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Saramaccan is analysed as a tone language with two contrastive level tones (high 'aigu' and low 'grave'), every syllable bearing a tone; the paper then describes tone sandhi ('perturbation'), the phrase-final lowering that closes the 'syntaxeme', and tonal word-structure constraints (no low syllable between highs inside a one-morph word). Word stress/accent placement is never described; the only accent statements are the explicit typological contrast with Sranan ('langue a accent avec accent sur le mot', p. 156) and the remark that a handful of irregular reduplications (biibii, sakasaka, kasikaasi, kesikesi) follow Sranan word-accent formation and are taken to be Sranan loans.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 156: a small group of reduplications with a single high syllable 'suivent completement les principes de formation du mot dans le Sranan, langue a accent avec accent sur le mot' and are judged borrowed from Sranan; intensifier words (faan, gbolo, kololoo) have anomalous all-high tone structures with an extensible final syllable (pp. 151-152).
new_statements.identity_note: All three works concern the Upper Suriname River variety of Saramaccan (Voorhoeve: 'Haut Surinam', material largely collected by A. Donicie; Glock: upper Suriname River, SIL fieldwork since 1968), the same variety as Rountree 1972 in the existing statement.

tone_statements.citation: Kramer, Marvin. 2004. High tone spread in Saramaccan serial verb constructions. Journal of Portuguese Linguistics 3(2): 31ff. Lisboa: Associacao Portuguesa de Linguistica / (now) Open Library of Humanities. DOI 10.5334/jpl.10.
tone_statements.quote: Saramaccan has features of a tone language, such as minimal tonal pairs. But there are only about 14 such pairs, and the contrasts are mainly between two types of words, items with all specified tones and items with unspecified tones, such as bɔ̀sɔ̀ ‘to loosen’ and bɔ́sɔ ‘brush’, or jàà ‘to splash’ and jáa ‘year’, but also mì ‘I’ in (1a) and mí ‘my’ in (1b) ... The use of tone in SM has little morphological or lexical function. But the contrasting tones for pronouns in (1a) and (1b), described in Voorhoeve (1961:161), are examples of both inflectional and the grammatical use of tone ... SM, then, has a tonal contrast alone for all pronouns except 3rd sg.
tone_statements.summary: TBUs are lexically H, L or unspecified; unspecified TBUs get H by sandhi spread (leftward; rightward in serial verbs), else L. Author, after Good 2004, leaves tone vs pitch accent typing open.

tone_statements.citation: Kramer, Marvin Gould. 2002. Substrate transfer in Saramaccan Creole. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. x+653 pp. (UMI/ProQuest AAT 3082261; DAI-A 64/02:483.)
tone_statements.quote: Saramaccan is a tone language. As such, it exhibits a characteristic of tone languages, namely tone sandhi. The tone of one tone-bearing unit, TBU, may spread to another. ... That SM is a tone language may be seen in a few minimal pairs: (51) ... e. mà but f. má I-NEG (Libase dialect) ... w. tù also x. tú two ... The SM lexicon is perhaps unique in having both tone and stress characteristics (Good 2001), including items where some or all syllables are specified with low tones ... Basically, syllables with unspecified tone have a default low tone. In a domain of tone sandhi, these unspecified syllables have a high tone between two syllables with specified high tone.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 238-240, sec. 4.6 and 4.6.1 Tone sandhi; last two sentences from pp. 48-49, sec. 2.2.1
tone_statements.summary: Tone language: lexical high (acute), low (grave), plus syllables unspecified for tone (default low, raised in sandhi domains); no explicit count; floating H proposed p. 256; stress traits per Good.

tone_statements.citation: Voorhoeve, Jan. 1959. An orthography for Saramaccan. Word 15(3): 436-445. DOI 10.1080/00437956.1959.11659707.
tone_statements.quote: One can distinguish two tone levels— ´ (high) and ` (low)—and three tone contours: low-high (ˇ), high-low (ˆ), and low-high-low (ˇ`). Moreover, vowel length appears to be distinctive. ... The high tone level is marked by an acute accent (´), while the low tone level is left unmarked. Tone contours are represented as sequences of level tones over repetitions of the vowel, thus: [màká] =/màká/ maká 'thorn' [mà·ká] =/mààká/ maaká 'to notice' [mǎ·kà] =/màákà/ maáka 'portent' ... The analysis of long vowels as combinations of short vowels each with its own tone is supported by the behavior of tones in situations where vowels belonging to separate morphemes are contracted.
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H/L; three surface contours analysed as H/L sequences on long vowels (p. 438 'contours as sequences of levels'). Final lowering, tone sandhi; at least 22 forms + tone-marked text.

tone_statements.citation: Steien, Guri Bordal & Kofi Yakpo. 2020. Romancing with tone: On the outcomes of prosodic contact. Language 96(1): 1-41. doi:10.1353/lan.2020.0000
tone_statements.quote: Saramaccan, a creole spoken by the descendants of Africans who established independent polities in the Amazonian rainforests of Suriname in the seventeenth century, has a prosodic system with two tones and numerous tonal processes (Rountree 1972, Good 2004). Portuguese- and English-sourced words have an H tone on the syllable that bears stress in the lexifier; compare wómì /HL/ 'man' (< Port. ˈhomem 'man') and àkí /LH/ 'here' (< Port. aˈqui 'here') (examples from Good 2009). [p. 25]

tone_statements.citation: Grimes, Joseph E. (1972). The Phonological Structure of Stems in Saramaccan. In Languages of the Guianas.
tone_statements.quote: Every vowel carries one tone. Two tones, high and low, are contrastive: témbé 'build', sémbé 'people', lémbé 'lick'. In long syllables the tones may be HL, kaima 'alligator', HH matuitui 'spotted sandpiper', LH noiti 'never', or LL peika 'fix'. In the most common stem pattern, one and only one syllable has a high tone: waka 'walk', fuuku 'early', siki/si 'six', apeesina 'orange'. A less common stem pattern has no high tone: vuNvuN 'hummingbird', logoso 'turtle', legede 'lie', sembe 'people', gbamba 'meat', maisi 'electric eel'. A third stem pattern has more than one high tone: matuitui 'spotted sandpiper', bumbuu 'state of well-being'. The stress pattern of stems can be predicted according to the following rules. (1) The first long syllable in each foot of the stem is stressed. (2) If there is no long syllable, the next to the last syllable in the phonological foot is stressed. In simple stems that correspond to more than one phonological foot, the first stress is the heaviest. Compound stems remain to be investigated. Two-syllable stems with a LH tone pattern have no set pattern; the stress varies freely between the syllables: 'bebé ~ be'bé 'drink', 'guli ~ gu'li 'swallow', 'kini

sources.note: Lexicon is split: classes (i)-(iii) are fully tone-specified (H/L contrastive, minimal pairs) and show no stress effects; the majority class (iv) carries one lexically placed pitch accent (realized as H, contrastive position: bigí vs bígi), from which stress is derived by parsing into trochaic feet from the leftmost H TBU (primary stress near the left edge, alternating secondary). Rountree 1972b's weight/penult-of-foot rule is quoted on p. 14 and reinterpreted. This is the catalog's deciding source; the catalog quote is verbatim from it.

sources.citation: Good, Jeff. 2009. A twice-mixed creole? Tracing the history of a prosodic split in the Saramaccan lexicon. Studies in Language 33:459-498 (author preprint, 51 pp).
sources.quote: 'as discussed in Good (2004b:586-594), the former class of words [pitch-accented] exhibit effects which can be associated with stress while the latter [truly tonal] does not. Furthermore, the realization of stress in the pitch-accented words is predictable based on the location of pitch accent ... Words with TBU's unspecified for tone show two surface manifestations of accent, pitch accent and stress. Words fully specified for tone show no evidence for being marked for accent at all.'

sources.note: Historical paper (why the accent/tone split arose after marronage); it restates the synchronic analysis of Good 2004: pitch accent words have stress predictable from the accent position (antepenultimate accent realized as HH spread, cf. hákísi, minísíti), tonal words have no stress. sources.citation: Good, Jeff. 2004/2005. Split prosody and creole simplicity: the case of Saramaccan. Journal of Portuguese Linguistics 3(2).
sources.quote: The correlation between pitch accent and stress is not completely trivial—that is, it is not simply the case that the stressed syllable is the same as the syllable containing the vowel marked with a high tone. However, it is predictable and, as discussed in Good (2004:588–592), can be straightforwardly analyzed using an algorithm that (i) parses words marked for accent into trochaic feet based on the position of the lexically-specified accent mark and (ii) assigns stress to the leftmost trochaic foot (with the result that stress is always found near the beginning of the word even if accent is not).
sources.note: Cleanest one-sentence statement of the Good analysis, with stress-marked forms: ˈnáki, foˈló, ˈíngísi, siˈkífi, ˈmɔkisá, miˈnísíti, ˈafokáti, aˈlukutú; stress diagnostics are high-vowel syncope in unstressed syllables (mɔkisá → mɔksá) and emphatic lengthening in stressed ones (sákása → sá:kása).

sources.quote: C'est la seule langue creole connue jusqu'a l'heure actuelle dans laquelle le ton est nettement distinctif. [...] le systeme complique qui comprend deux niveaux de ton, trois contours de ton et la duree des voyelles peut s'analyser comme un systeme de deux niveaux de tons (aigu et grave) relativement tres simple, dans lequel chaque syllabe ou mot doit porter un niveau du ton. sources.citation: Kramer, Marvin. 2004. High tone spread in Saramaccan serial verb constructions. Journal of Portuguese Linguistics 3(2): 31ff. Lisboa: Associacao Portuguesa de Linguistica / (now) Open Library of Humanities. DOI 10.5334/jpl.10.
sources.quote: Saramaccan has features of a tone language, such as minimal tonal pairs. But there are only about 14 such pairs, and the contrasts are mainly between two types of words, items with all specified tones and items with unspecified tones, such as bɔ̀sɔ̀ ‘to loosen’ and bɔ́sɔ ‘brush’, or jàà ‘to splash’ and jáa ‘year’, but also mì ‘I’ in (1a) and mí ‘my’ in (1b) ... The use of tone in SM has little morphological or lexical function. But the contrasting tones for pronouns in (1a) and (1b), described in Voorhoeve (1961:161), are examples of both inflectional and the grammatical use of tone ... SM, then, has a tonal contrast alone for all pronouns except 3rd sg.
sources.note: TBUs are lexically H, L or unspecified; unspecified TBUs get H by sandhi spread (leftward; rightward in serial verbs), else L. Author, after Good 2004, leaves tone vs pitch accent typing open.

sources.citation: Kramer, Marvin Gould. 2002. Substrate transfer in Saramaccan Creole. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. x+653 pp. (UMI/ProQuest AAT 3082261; DAI-A 64/02:483.)
sources.quote: Saramaccan is a tone language. As such, it exhibits a characteristic of tone languages, namely tone sandhi. The tone of one tone-bearing unit, TBU, may spread to another. ... That SM is a tone language may be seen in a few minimal pairs: (51) ... e. mà but f. má I-NEG (Libase dialect) ... w. tù also x. tú two ... The SM lexicon is perhaps unique in having both tone and stress characteristics (Good 2001), including items where some or all syllables are specified with low tones ... Basically, syllables with unspecified tone have a default low tone. In a domain of tone sandhi, these unspecified syllables have a high tone between two syllables with specified high tone.
sources.locator: pp. 238-240, sec. 4.6 and 4.6.1 Tone sandhi; last two sentences from pp. 48-49, sec. 2.2.1
sources.note: Tone language: lexical high (acute), low (grave), plus syllables unspecified for tone (default low, raised in sandhi domains); no explicit count; floating H proposed p. 256; stress traits per Good.

sources.quote: One can distinguish two tone levels— ´ (high) and ` (low)—and three tone contours: low-high (ˇ), high-low (ˆ), and low-high-low (ˇ`). Moreover, vowel length appears to be distinctive. ... The high tone level is marked by an acute accent (´), while the low tone level is left unmarked. Tone contours are represented as sequences of level tones over repetitions of the vowel, thus: [màká] =/màká/ maká 'thorn' [mà·ká] =/mààká/ maaká 'to notice' [mǎ·kà] =/màákà/ maáka 'portent' ... The analysis of long vowels as combinations of short vowels each with its own tone is supported by the behavior of tones in situations where vowels belonging to separate morphemes are contracted.
sources.note: Two level tones H/L; three surface contours analysed as H/L sequences on long vowels (p. 438 'contours as sequences of levels'). Final lowering, tone sandhi; at least 22 forms + tone-marked text.
